meta.title: Longevity research — a category map
meta.description: Categories of longevity research cut by what a piece of work does for the goal, in three levels: six functions (mechanisms, measurement, interventions, translation, research accelerants, preservation and substrate) -> 26 groups -> 78 classes, with ~1,400 recent works hanging under the classes as evidence. Colour is the group's kind: green technology and interfaces, red therapeutics, blue preservation, lime biology, measurement and translation. Around them, on outer orbits: purple researchers, brown institutions, gold grant givers, orange companies. Dark grey works are retracted or report a null result.

weight.metric: categories: thousands of works, 2018-2026, whose title carries the category's own terms and whose abstract names aging. funders: units of US$10M committed to the works on THIS map, each award at its most recent fiscal year (NIH RePORTER) — not the body's total budget. funders with no award-level amounts, and every company, are drawn at a declared floor size, because their money is unknown rather than small.
weight.note: Attention, not money or quality. A small number is a thin literature: it can be underexplored, or it can be a dead end — the boundary sentence and the colour are what tell them apart.

meta.brief: Which parts of longevity research are structurally thin, and where does the money sit against the literature?

nodes.label: Mechanisms of aging
nodes.desc: The whole map is cut by what a piece of work does for the goal, not by discipline, by mechanism or by who runs it. This root is the first function: general knowledge of why bodies decline, cut by level of biological organisation. Not here: a number about one body (Measurement and diagnosis) and not a way to change a trajectory (Interventions). Test: can you state the lesion, state or determinant the work establishes, without naming the person it was measured in?

nodes.label: Molecular damage and maintenance failure
nodes.desc: Lesions and the machinery that should clear them, at the level of a molecule, a complex or an organelle. Not here: a drug that restores clearance (Pharmacology and small molecules) and not a blood marker of the lesion (Biological age clocks). Test: does the work name a molecule, complex or organelle as the thing that fails?

nodes.label: Proteostasis and chaperone failure
nodes.desc: Misfolding, aggregation and the chaperone and ubiquitin systems that should prevent them. Not here: autophagy, which is the bulk-degradation route (see Autophagy and mitophagy), and not a proteostasis drug (Pharmacology and small molecules). Test: is the failure a protein that will not fold or be refolded?

nodes.label: Autophagy and mitophagy
nodes.desc: Bulk degradation: autophagosome formation, lysosomal clearance, and the selective removal of mitochondria. Not here: a single misfolded protein's fate (Proteostasis) and not a fasting protocol that raises autophagy (Caloric restriction and fasting). Test: is the mechanism the removal of material in bulk, rather than the folding of one protein?

nodes.label: Mitochondrial dysfunction
nodes.desc: Respiratory chain failure, mtDNA mutation burden, ROS production and the retrograde signalling that follows. Not here: mitophagy as a clearance route (Autophagy and mitophagy) and not a mitochondrial-targeted supplement (Pharmacology and small molecules). Test: does the finding originate in the organelle's own machinery?

nodes.label: DNA damage and repair
nodes.desc: Lesion formation, repair-pathway choice, and the senescence or death that follows an unrepaired break. Not here: telomere attrition as a separate mechanism and not an epigenetic mark (Epigenetic drift and loss of identity). Test: is the lesion a break, adduct or mutation in the DNA itself?

nodes.label: Cell states
nodes.desc: States a single cell enters and keeps, as against a lesion in one of its molecules. Not here: a protocol that forces a cell out of the state (Genetic and epigenetic therapy) and not a score computed from it (Biological age clocks). Test: is the finding a state a cell is in, described without a way to reverse it?

nodes.label: Cellular senescence
nodes.desc: Arrest, the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, and the markers that identify the state in vivo. Not here: a senolytic that removes the cell (Senolytics) and not an SASP-blocking drug (Senomorphics and SASP modulators). Test: does the work establish that the cell is senescent, rather than what to do about it?

nodes.label: Stem-cell exhaustion
nodes.desc: Loss of stem-cell number, potency and asymmetric division with age, and the niche that fails around them. Not here: transplanting new stem cells (Stem-cell therapy) and not the differentiation programme as a mechanism of identity (Epigenetic drift). Test: is the finding a decline in the pool or its output?

nodes.label: Epigenetic drift and loss of identity
nodes.desc: Methylation landscape drift, loss of the transcriptional programme that says what a cell is, and the clocks that read that drift. Not here: a clock used as a measurement (Methylation clocks) and not a reprogramming protocol (Partial reprogramming). Test: is the claim that the cell's programme has drifted, rather than that a clock reads older?

nodes.label: Signalling between organs
nodes.desc: Failures that exist only between cells, tissues or organs. Not here: a single-cell mechanism (Cell states) and not a systemic drug (Pharmacology and small molecules). Test: would the finding disappear if every cell were studied alone?

nodes.label: Inflammaging
nodes.desc: Low-grade, sterile, chronic inflammation as a driver of age-related disease. Not here: the immune system's own decline (Immunosenescence) and not a SASP-blocking drug (Senomorphics and SASP modulators). Test: is the signal an inflammatory mediator acting on tissue, rather than a failing immune cell?

nodes.label: Immunosenescence
nodes.desc: Thymic involution, clonal exhaustion, and the loss of naive repertoire. Not here: inflammation as a tissue signal (Inflammaging) and not an engineered immune cell (CAR-T and immune-cell therapy). Test: is the failing component an immune cell's function?

nodes.label: Gut microbiome and host aging
nodes.desc: Compositional change with age, its metabolites, and the barrier and immune consequences. Not here: an inflammatory mediator downstream (Inflammaging) and not a probiotic sold as a geroprotector (Pharmacology and small molecules). Test: does the finding originate in the microbial community?

nodes.label: Vascular aging
nodes.desc: Endothelial failure, arterial stiffening, and the perfusion deficit that ages every organ downstream. Not here: matrix cross-linking as a molecular lesion (Proteostasis and chaperone failure) and not a blood-pressure drug (Pharmacology and small molecules). Test: is the lesion in the vessel wall or the flow?

nodes.label: Genetic determinants of lifespan
nodes.desc: What sets the rate rather than what accumulates. Not here: an intervention that acts on the pathway in a patient (Pharmacology and small molecules) and not a comparison across species (Comparative and evolutionary longevity). Test: does the work name a gene, variant or programme whose alteration predicts a change in lifespan?

nodes.label: Nutrient-sensing pathways
nodes.desc: mTOR, insulin/IGF-1, AMPK and sirtuins as the pathways that transduce food supply into growth, repair and lifespan. Not here: a drug that acts on them (Rapamycin and mTOR inhibitors, Metformin and biguanides) and not a dietary protocol (Caloric restriction and fasting). Test: does the work establish pathway behaviour as a determinant, rather than administer something?

nodes.label: Human longevity genetics
nodes.desc: Variants, polygenic scores and centenarian cohorts that associate with exceptional survival. Not here: a model organism's mutant (the pathway work above) and not a methylation clock (Methylation clocks). Test: does the claim rest on a human genotype?

nodes.label: Comparative and evolutionary longevity
nodes.desc: Why species differ — bats, mole-rats, whales, hydra — and the evolutionary theory that explains it. Not here: a human variant (Human longevity genetics) and not population statistics (The LEV account). Test: does the work compare two species, or explain why a lifespan is the length it is?

nodes.label: Measurement and diagnosis
nodes.desc: Turning the state of a body into numbers that can be acted on and re-measured, cut by the scale of the thing measured. Not here: the mechanism a measurement is built on (Mechanisms of aging) and not a measurement used as a trial outcome (Endpoint qualification). Test: does the output belong to a named person or cohort, in a unit you could quote back to them?

nodes.label: Biological age clocks
nodes.desc: Estimators that turn a biosample into an age or a pace. Not here: the mechanism a clock is built on (Mechanisms of aging) and not a clock being judged as a trial outcome (Endpoint qualification). Test: does the output claim to be an age, a pace or a mortality probability?

nodes.label: Methylation clocks
nodes.desc: CpG-based estimators, their training sets and their replication. Not here: the drift they measure as a mechanism (Epigenetic drift and loss of identity). Test: is the estimator built from methylation?

nodes.label: Proteomic and metabolomic clocks
nodes.desc: Age estimators from proteins, metabolites or composites of both. Not here: a methylation estimator (Methylation clocks). Test: is the input a protein or metabolite panel?

nodes.label: Pace of aging
nodes.desc: Estimators of the rate rather than the level — how fast a body is changing per year. Not here: a clock that reports an age (Methylation clocks). Test: is the output a slope rather than a value?

nodes.label: Organ-level functional assessment
nodes.desc: How well a named organ is working. Not here: a whole-body molecular clock (Biological age clocks) and not a device aimed at finding one disease early (Early warning). Test: can you name the organ whose function the measurement reports?

nodes.label: Organ age from imaging
nodes.desc: Imaging and function tests that report an organ's apparent age or deficit. Not here: a multi-organ plasma score (Proteomic and metabolomic clocks). Test: is the report about a named organ?

nodes.label: Frailty and functional reserve
nodes.desc: Frailty indices, gait, grip and reserve measures that predict decline without naming a disease. Not here: a molecular clock (Biological age clocks). Test: is the measure a capacity to function?

nodes.label: Early warning and points of no return
nodes.desc: Finding the first irreversible step — the threshold after which a lesion is no longer repairable. Not here: a general clock (Biological age clocks) and not a test of organ function (Organ-level functional assessment). Test: does the work identify a crossing that changes what treatment is still possible?

nodes.label: Liquid biopsy
nodes.desc: Blood-borne detection of a developing lesion — circulating DNA, cells and vesicles. Not here: a wearable (Continuous and wearable sensing) and not a methylation clock (Methylation clocks). Test: is the signal a shed fragment in a body fluid?

nodes.label: Continuous and wearable sensing
nodes.desc: Devices that sample a body continuously and the models that read them. Not here: an imaging threshold (Pre-symptomatic imaging). Test: does the data arrive without a clinic visit?

nodes.label: Pre-symptomatic imaging
nodes.desc: Imaging and screening aimed at the state before diagnosis. Not here: a blood test (Liquid biopsy) and not a functional-capacity score (Frailty and functional reserve). Test: does the finding predate symptoms?

nodes.label: Population mortality and the LEV account
nodes.desc: The demography that turns the goal into arithmetic. Not here: a per-person clock (Biological age clocks) and not the endpoint that licenses a drug (Endpoint qualification). Test: is the unit a population and a year?

nodes.label: The LEV account
nodes.desc: Years of life expectancy gained per calendar year, and the arithmetic that defines an escape velocity. Not here: a trial endpoint (Endpoint qualification). Test: is the claim a rate of gain against time?

nodes.label: Compression of morbidity
nodes.desc: Whether added years are healthy years — the healthspan and disability-free-life-expectancy literature. Not here: the escape-velocity arithmetic (The LEV account). Test: is the measure years lived without disability?

nodes.label: Interventions
nodes.desc: The things supposed to change a trajectory rather than describe it, cut by what the intervention acts on: a molecule, the genome, a cell, an organ, a behaviour. Not here: the biology an intervention exploits (Mechanisms of aging) and not the route that gets it licensed (Translation and clinical machinery). Test: could the work be summarised as a protocol with a dose, a vector, a cell product or a behaviour?

nodes.label: Pharmacology and small molecules
nodes.desc: Molecules meant to slow or reverse aging as such, split by their target class. Not here: a gene or cell therapy (Genetic and epigenetic therapy, Cell and tissue replacement) and not a lifestyle protocol (Behavioural and environmental intervention). Test: is the thing administered a molecule with a dose and a named target?

nodes.label: Senolytics
nodes.desc: Drugs that kill senescent cells — BCL-2 family inhibitors, dasatinib plus quercetin, fisetin. Not here: drugs that leave the cell alive and quieten it (Senomorphics and SASP modulators) and not the senescence biology itself (Cellular senescence). Test: does the compound reduce the senescent-cell load by killing them?

nodes.label: NAD+ precursors
nodes.desc: NAD+ repletion by precursor supplementation — NMN, NR, nicotinamide — and the enzymes that consume NAD+. Not here: a sirtuin activator that does not raise NAD+ (Nutrient-sensing pathways for the biology) and not metformin (Metformin and biguanides). Test: is the administered thing a NAD+ precursor?

nodes.label: Rapamycin and mTOR inhibitors
nodes.desc: mTOR inhibition as a lifespan intervention, its dosing and its immune cost. Not here: the pathway as a determinant (Nutrient-sensing pathways). Test: is the intervention mTOR inhibition?

nodes.label: Metformin and biguanides
nodes.desc: Biguanides repurposed for aging, and the trials trying to establish a geroprotective effect. Not here: the aging-as-indication regulatory problem (Regulatory science and indications). Test: is the molecule a biguanide?

nodes.label: Senomorphics and SASP modulators
nodes.desc: Compounds and interventions that suppress the senescent secretome without killing the cell. Not here: senolytics (Senolytics). Test: does the cell survive while its output is suppressed?

nodes.label: Genetic and epigenetic therapy
nodes.desc: Writes to the genome or its regulation. Not here: a small molecule (Pharmacology and small molecules) and not cells grown outside the body (Cell and tissue replacement). Test: does the intervention change the sequence or the regulation of a cell's own DNA?

nodes.label: Gene therapy and editing
nodes.desc: Adding, correcting or disabling a gene in a living body, and the delivery problem that decides whether it works. Not here: partial reprogramming (Partial reprogramming) and not a cell edited outside the body (CAR-T and immune-cell therapy). Test: is a sequence in the patient's own cells being changed?

nodes.label: Partial reprogramming
nodes.desc: Transient expression of reprogramming factors to reverse age-associated change without erasing identity. Not here: the identity drift it tries to reverse (Epigenetic drift and loss of identity). Test: are reprogramming factors being delivered, transiently?

nodes.label: Epigenetic editing
nodes.desc: Writing or erasing a methylation or histone mark without changing the sequence. Not here: a full reprogramming protocol (Partial reprogramming). Test: is the edit to a mark rather than to a base?

nodes.label: Cell and tissue replacement
nodes.desc: New biological material put into the body. Not here: replacing the whole organ (Organ replacement and mechanical substitution) and not a drug the cells respond to (Pharmacology and small molecules). Test: is the delivered thing a living cell or a tissue construct?

nodes.label: Stem-cell therapy
nodes.desc: Transplanted stem or progenitor populations, their sourcing and their engraftment. Not here: the aged pool's decline (Stem-cell exhaustion). Test: are cells being given to a patient?

nodes.label: CAR-T and immune-cell therapy
nodes.desc: Engineered immune cells, including those aimed at senescent or fibrotic tissue. Not here: the immune system's own decline (Immunosenescence). Test: are the cells engineered rather than merely collected?

nodes.label: Tissue engineering and organoids
nodes.desc: Growing tissue constructs and organoids for replacement or as test beds. Not here: whole-organ substitution (Organ replacement and mechanical substitution) and not an assay-platform use (Organ-on-chip as a test bed). Test: is the output a living construct?

nodes.label: Organ replacement and mechanical substitution
nodes.desc: Taking over an organ's function rather than repairing its cells. Not here: tissue grown in a dish (Tissue engineering and organoids) and not a device that only reports function (Organ-level functional assessment). Test: does the intervention carry the organ's function, not just its reading?

nodes.label: Xenotransplantation
nodes.desc: Genetically edited animal organs placed in a human, and the rejection biology that follows. Not here: a human donor organ preserved longer (Machine perfusion). Test: is the organ from another species?

nodes.label: Bioartificial organs
nodes.desc: Devices with living components that stand in for an organ's function. Not here: a wholly mechanical pump (Implantable assist devices). Test: does the device contain living cells?

nodes.label: Implantable assist devices
nodes.desc: Mechanical pumps, stimulators and implants that take over a failing function. Not here: a neurostimulator for a brain interface (Neuromodulation and memory prosthetics). Test: is the device mechanical or electronic and replacing a body function?

nodes.label: Behavioural and environmental intervention
nodes.desc: Interventions performed by the person rather than administered to them. Not here: a molecule that mimics fasting or exercise (Pharmacology and small molecules — the pill goes there whatever it mimics). Test: could the effect be obtained without the subject doing or being exposed to anything?

nodes.label: Exercise protocols
nodes.desc: Training regimes, dose and the molecular response to them in older adults. Not here: a molecule that mimics exercise (Pharmacology and small molecules). Test: is the intervention a training protocol?

nodes.label: Caloric restriction and fasting
nodes.desc: Reduced intake and fasting windows, and the trials that measure their effect in humans. Not here: a fasting mimetic (Pharmacology and small molecules). Test: is the intervention a change in when or how much the subject eats?

nodes.label: Diet composition and nutrition
nodes.desc: What is eaten rather than how much: patterns, micronutrients, protein level. Not here: total intake restriction (Caloric restriction and fasting). Test: is the variable the composition of the diet?

nodes.label: Sleep
nodes.desc: Sleep duration, architecture and disorder as an aging exposure, and the interventions that change them. Not here: a sedative's pharmacology (Pharmacology and small molecules). Test: is the exposure sleep itself?

nodes.label: Translation and clinical machinery
nodes.desc: The machinery that decides whether a working intervention reaches people, cut by pipeline stage. Not here: the intervention itself (Interventions) and not capital, deals or clinic business models — a funding vehicle is not a research category. Test: would a better answer here shorten the time between a result in a model and a prescription?

nodes.label: Endpoint qualification
nodes.desc: What a trial measures when the outcome is decades away. Not here: a clock used to describe a person (Biological age clocks); here the clock is on trial. Test: is the work about whether a measure may stand in for a clinical result?

nodes.label: Surrogate endpoints
nodes.desc: Measures accepted in place of a hard outcome, and the evidence needed to accept them. Not here: the qualification procedure (Biomarker qualification). Test: is a measure standing in for an outcome?

nodes.label: Biomarker qualification
nodes.desc: The formal path from an association to an accepted, qualified biomarker. Not here: a clock's own construction (Biological age clocks). Test: is the work about a regulator or consortium accepting a marker?

nodes.label: Trial design and methodology
nodes.desc: How a geroscience hypothesis is tested in humans. Not here: what the trial measures (Endpoint qualification) and not what a regulator will accept (Regulatory science and indications). Test: is the contribution a design that changes what a trial can conclude?

nodes.label: Platform and adaptive trials
nodes.desc: Designs that test several arms under one protocol and update as data arrive. Not here: a single-agent design (n-of-1 and withdrawal designs). Test: is the contribution the trial's structure?

nodes.label: n-of-1 and withdrawal designs
nodes.desc: Single-subject and treatment-withdrawal designs for slow, heterogeneous effects. Not here: a multi-arm platform (Platform and adaptive trials). Test: is the unit of randomisation one person or one withdrawal?

nodes.label: Regulatory science and indications
nodes.desc: Whether aging can be an indication at all. Not here: how the evidence is generated (Trial design and methodology) and not the money that pays for it. Test: does the work argue what a regulator must accept?

nodes.label: Aging as an indication
nodes.desc: The argument that aging itself can be a target, and the disease proxies used when it cannot. Not here: a specific compound's approval (Approval pathways and accelerated approval). Test: does the work argue about what counts as the condition being treated?

nodes.label: Approval pathways and accelerated approval
nodes.desc: The routes a geroprotector can take through a regulator, and the conditions attached to each. Not here: the indication argument (Aging as an indication). Test: is the subject a procedural route through an agency?

nodes.label: Preclinical validity and model bridging
nodes.desc: How much a model predicts a human. Not here: a model used to discover a mechanism (In-silico models) and not the design of the human trial (Trial design and methodology). Test: is the question whether the result would hold in a human?

nodes.label: Mouse-to-human translation
nodes.desc: Where mouse results fail to hold in people, and the strain and husbandry choices that decide it. Not here: a primate study (Primate models). Test: is the model a rodent?

nodes.label: Organ-on-chip as a test bed
nodes.desc: Microfluidic human tissue used to test a candidate before a person. Not here: organoids grown for replacement (Tissue engineering and organoids). Test: is the construct used to test rather than to implant?

nodes.label: Primate models
nodes.desc: Non-human primate studies of aging and of candidate interventions. Not here: a rodent study (Mouse-to-human translation). Test: is the model a primate?

nodes.label: Long-horizon safety and real-world evidence
nodes.desc: Evidence that only exists after approval. Not here: pre-approval trial design (Trial design and methodology) and not a population mortality trend (Population mortality and the LEV account). Test: is the data generated while the product is already in use?

nodes.label: Pharmacovigilance
nodes.desc: Detecting slow or rare harms in a population already taking the drug. Not here: a trial's safety endpoint (Trial design and methodology). Test: is the signal collected after marketing?

nodes.label: Real-world evidence
nodes.desc: Cohorts, registries and claims data used to answer questions a trial did not ask. Not here: a pharmacovigilance signal (Pharmacovigilance). Test: is the data observational and post-approval?

nodes.label: Research accelerants
nodes.desc: Technology whose purpose is to make the other roots faster and cheaper, cut by which part of the research loop it accelerates. Not here: a device used on a patient (Measurement and diagnosis) and not a technology that is itself the therapy (Interventions). Test: does the work change the cost or speed of producing knowledge?

nodes.label: In-silico models of cells and organisms
nodes.desc: Simulating a mechanism rather than fitting a pattern. Not here: a statistical model learned from data with no mechanism inside (Machine learning over biological data). Test: does the artefact simulate a mechanism, with state variables you could inspect?

nodes.label: Virtual cell
nodes.desc: A computable model of a cell's own machinery, from metabolism to gene regulation. Not here: a learned predictor of cell state (Foundation models over cells). Test: does the model have the cell's mechanisms in it?

nodes.label: Patient and organ digital twins
nodes.desc: A calibrated model of one patient or organ, used to try a treatment before giving it. Not here: a model of a cell (Virtual cell). Test: is the model fitted to an individual?

nodes.label: Molecular dynamics and docking
nodes.desc: Physics-based simulation of a molecule's behaviour, used to choose what to make. Not here: a learned structure predictor (Structure prediction and design). Test: does the method integrate forces over time?

nodes.label: Machine learning over biological data
nodes.desc: Learned functions that predict from data. Not here: a mechanistic simulator (In-silico models) and not the automation that produces the training data (High-throughput and automated experimentation). Test: is the contribution a function learned from data and evaluated on held-out data?

nodes.label: Foundation models over cells and text
nodes.desc: Large pretrained models over expression, perturbation or the literature, and their transfer. Not here: a structure predictor (Structure prediction and design). Test: is the model pretrained on a broad corpus and then adapted?

nodes.label: Structure prediction and design
nodes.desc: Predicting and inverting protein structure to make a binder or an enzyme. Not here: physics-based simulation (Molecular dynamics and docking). Test: is the output a structure or a sequence design?

nodes.label: Target discovery from data
nodes.desc: Mining omics, literature and networks to name a protein worth hitting. Not here: a model of the cell (Virtual cell). Test: does the work end in a named target?

nodes.label: High-throughput and automated experimentation
nodes.desc: More conditions per person-hour. Not here: a computational model of the screen (Machine learning over biological data) and not a device used on a patient (Early warning). Test: does the work multiply the number of conditions tested per unit of labour?

nodes.label: Self-driving laboratories
nodes.desc: Closed-loop robot plus model systems that choose the next experiment. Not here: a passive high-content screen (High-content screening). Test: does the system decide what to run next?

nodes.label: High-content screening
nodes.desc: Screens that put thousands of conditions through one assay, and the statistics that keep them honest. Not here: an autonomous loop (Self-driving laboratories). Test: is the contribution throughput on a fixed assay?

nodes.label: Data infrastructure and standards
nodes.desc: The shared substrate other groups build on. Not here: a model trained on that data (Machine learning over biological data) and not the statistics read off it (Population mortality and the LEV account). Test: is the contribution something another group must use to do its own work?

nodes.label: Biobanks and cohorts
nodes.desc: Stored samples and followed populations that others draw from. Not here: a single study's own samples. Test: is the resource reused by other groups?

nodes.label: Ontologies and metadata standards
nodes.desc: Controlled vocabularies, schemas and sharing rules that make data comparable. Not here: the cohort itself (Biobanks and cohorts). Test: does the work define how data is described?

nodes.label: Preservation and substrate
nodes.desc: Research that assumes the biology will not be fixed in time and works on the person instead, cut by what happens to the person: stop the whole clock, keep the organ, connect the brain to a machine, move the mind off the brain. Not here: anything that repairs aging in a living body (Interventions) and not a device that only measures (Measurement and diagnosis). Test: does the work proceed by storing, preserving, interfacing with or copying, rather than by treating?

nodes.label: Whole-organism cryopreservation
nodes.desc: Stopping biological time in a whole body. Not here: keeping a single organ for transplant (Organ banking and reperfusion). Test: is the unit preserved the entire organism, held to be revived later?

nodes.label: Whole-body vitrification
nodes.desc: Ice-free preservation of an entire organism at cryogenic temperature. Not here: a single organ (Sub-zero organ storage). Test: is the preserved object a whole body?

nodes.label: Cryoprotectants and toxicity
nodes.desc: The chemistry that replaces water without killing the tissue, and its own toxicity. Not here: the cooling hardware (Nanowarming and rewarming). Test: is the subject what is added to the tissue?

nodes.label: Nanowarming and rewarming
nodes.desc: Getting heat back into a vitrified organ fast enough to avoid fracture and ice. Not here: the solution itself (Cryoprotectants and toxicity). Test: is the problem the rate and uniformity of warming?

nodes.label: Cryonics practice and storage
nodes.desc: The practice around suspension: custody, audit, legal status, and what a patient actually buys. Not here: the science of vitrification (Whole-body vitrification). Test: is the subject the arrangement rather than the biology?

nodes.label: Organ banking and reperfusion
nodes.desc: Preserving and restoring one organ outside a body. Not here: whole-body storage (Whole-organism cryopreservation) and not a device that replaces the organ's function (Organ replacement). Test: is the organ kept alive or restored outside the body?

nodes.label: Machine perfusion
nodes.desc: Pumping oxygenated fluid through an organ to keep it viable outside a body. Not here: freezing it (Sub-zero organ storage). Test: is the organ being perfused?

nodes.label: Sub-zero organ storage
nodes.desc: Keeping an organ below zero without ice, and the rewarming that follows. Not here: warm perfusion (Machine perfusion). Test: is the storage temperature below freezing?

nodes.label: Ischemia-reperfusion injury
nodes.desc: The damage done by cutting and restoring blood supply, the limit on every preservation method. Not here: the storage technology (Sub-zero organ storage). Test: is the injury caused by the loss and return of flow?

nodes.label: Human-brain interfaces (HBI)
nodes.desc: A channel between nervous tissue and a machine, cut by how the channel is made. Not here: mapping the brain's wiring without an implanted channel (Whole-brain emulation) and not a device that measures aging (Measurement and diagnosis). Test: does the work put a channel between nervous tissue and a machine?

nodes.label: Intracortical arrays
nodes.desc: Penetrating electrode arrays in cortex, their yield, and the glial scarring that ends their life. Not here: a surface or vessel route (ECoG and endovascular interfaces). Test: is the electrode inside the brain tissue?

nodes.label: ECoG and endovascular interfaces
nodes.desc: Surface and blood-vessel routes that trade bandwidth for stability and safety. Not here: a penetrating array (Intracortical arrays). Test: is the electrode on the surface or in a vessel?

nodes.label: Non-invasive BCI (EEG, fNIRS)
nodes.desc: Interfaces that read the brain from outside the skull, and the decoding that has to fight the skull. Not here: an implanted channel (Intracortical arrays, ECoG and endovascular interfaces). Test: is the sensor outside the body?

nodes.label: Speech and language decoding
nodes.desc: Turning neural activity into text or synthesized speech at usable rates. Not here: motor control of a limb or cursor (Motor and robotic prosthetics). Test: is the decoded output language?

nodes.label: Motor and robotic prosthetics
nodes.desc: Cursor, limb and exoskeleton control from cortical activity, and the feedback loop back. Not here: stimulation without a decoded command (Neuromodulation and memory prosthetics). Test: is a movement being commanded?

nodes.label: Neuromodulation and memory prosthetics
nodes.desc: Writing into the nervous system: stimulation for disease, mood and memory, and the closed-loop devices that do it. Not here: reading a command out (Motor and robotic prosthetics). Test: is the device stimulating rather than recording?

nodes.label: Whole-brain emulation and connectomics
nodes.desc: Turning a brain into a substrate-independent structure. Not here: a live interface that reads or writes (Human-brain interfaces). Test: is the target a map or a simulation of the whole brain, rather than a channel into a living one?

nodes.label: Connectomics
nodes.desc: Reconstructing the wiring diagram at synaptic resolution, and the proofreading that dominates the cost. Not here: a live interface (Intracortical arrays). Test: is the output a wiring map?

nodes.label: Emulation and whole-brain modelling
nodes.desc: Whether a mapped or modelled brain can be run, and what would count as evidence that it is the person. Not here: the mapping itself (Connectomics). Test: is the claim about running the structure?

nodes.label: Horvath 2013 — DNA methylation age of human tissues and cell types
nodes.desc: Establishes the boundary: an estimator that returns an age from methylation, with no mechanism claimed.

nodes.label: Gorgoulis et al. 2019 — Cellular Senescence: Defining a Path Forward
nodes.desc: Establishes the boundary: operational markers that make senescence a measurable cell state.

nodes.label: Franceschi et al. 2000 — Inflamm-aging: an evolutionary perspective on immunosenescence
nodes.desc: Establishes the boundary: aging as a between-organ signal — the category's test is that the finding vanishes when a cell is studied alone.

nodes.label: Kenyon et al. 1993 — A C. elegans mutant that lives twice as long as wild type
